findings.summary: The new `sequencer.close()` is the LAST statement of close()'s `finally` block, and it declares `throws IOException`. A `finally` that throws DISCARDS the exception from the `try`, so a failed final flush is silently replaced by the lease-release failure. This is the identical defect the same class already documents having fixed, eleven lines below the new code: drainPushes()'s javadoc (lines 438-444) reads "an unchecked throw from a finally escaped every catch (IOException) while masking a failed final flush", which is why drainPushes was deliberately made non-throwing -- and the new call is placed immediately after it in the same block. The codebase already has the right shape one file over: LocalSequencer.start (lines 119-123) wraps its own leases.release() and uses addSuppressed precisely for this pairing.
findings.failure_scenario: The object store is unreachable during a graceful pod shutdown. flushNow() throws IOException -- the final segment is not committed, which is the one failure this whole method exists to prevent. The finally block then runs sequencer.close() -> LeaseManager.release() -> store.putIfMatch against the same unreachable store, which throws, and that exception REPLACES the flush failure. The operator sees "lease release failed" and has no signal at all that the last segment was lost. A second, cheaper path reaches the same place with no store outage: drainPushes() sets Thread.currentThread().interrupt() when its pusher.join is interrupted, so the very next call, BoundedLock.takeOrFail -> lock.tryLock, throws InterruptedException immediately and is rethrown as IOException("interrupted waiting for the lease lock to release") -- masking the flush result AND leaving the lease unreleased, i.e. losing the ~10 s failover the added request was bought for.

findings.summary: The rationale given for choosing a real LocalSequencer over FakeSequencer -- repeated in three new places -- is checkably false, and in one of them it misstates what an ADR-0016 cost figure counts. (a) http/build.gradle.kts:21-23 justifies the new `testImplementation(testFixtures(project(":sequencer")))` with "the memory- and rate-sensitive tests here count a commit-log append among the requests they measure": NO test under http/src/test reads counts() at all -- BulkThroughTheRealStackTest:95 wraps a CountingBinStore and never queries it, and the two MemoryFlat* tests measure heap, not requests. All three touched http tests need only *a* Sequencer, and FakeSequencer (already in the fixture jar the author wired) would do. (b) sequencer/src/testFixtures/java/binjava/sequencer/TestSequencers.java:13-17 lists "IntervalPutRateTest against ADR-0016's table" as a test that counts requests through a Sequencer, and (c) ingest/src/test/java/binjava/ingest/IngestTestSupport.java:73-76 repeats it. IntervalPutRateTest constructs no DefaultIngest and no Sequencer -- it drives Accumulator + SegmentPublisher directly -- and its own class javadoc states the exact opposite in a warning: "ONLY SegmentPublisher, no CommitLog: ... a commit-log append is a SEPARATE request the cost table does not fold into that figure, and including it here would measure something the SPEC never claimed." The claim originates in the M4.6d backlog row, which this diff EDITS (line 258) and leaves standing; per sdd.md a spec found wrong is corrected, not copied into three files. The genuinely true reason for a real sequencer is narrower and is only the third item in TestSequencers' list: DefaultIngestTest's own request-delta assertions (isEqualTo(4) at lines 83, 254, 326, 345, 420) would each read 3 with a fake.
findings.failure_scenario: TestSequencers is a public fixture now on four modules' test classpaths, so its javadoc is where the next author bounding cost will look. Reading it, they conclude ADR-0016's PUT/s table folds in the commit-log append, and either restate the modelled PUT rate at 2/interval instead of 1/interval, or "fix" IntervalPutRateTest to include the commit -- changing the number M3 acceptance criterion 4 is asserted against, in the direction that hides a regression. Separately, someone adding a memory test to http reads build.gradle.kts:21, believes those tests measure request counts, and wires a real LocalSequencer into it -- paying a lease stat + putIfAbsent, a recover() LIST and a CONTINUE PUT and retaining those objects in MemoryBinStore (which "never frees a PUT") inside the 256 MB heap MemoryFlatUnderTenXBodySizeTest is deliberately run under, i.e. the crash-not-fail test AGENTS.md already records as invisible to check-tdd.

findings.summary: The constructor now takes `store`, `prefix` AND a pre-built `Sequencer`, and nothing checks that the sequencer addresses the same store and prefix. Before this change the CommitLog was built from the same store+prefix the SegmentPublisher uses, so a delta's segmentKey was always addressable from the store the delta lives in; that agreement was structural and is now a caller obligation with no check and no gate. This is the same gate-design rung-1 argument the diff itself makes for M4.6f, applied to a bad state the diff newly makes representable.
findings.failure_scenario: The wiring commit the task row anticipates builds LocalSequencer over the cluster prefix and DefaultIngest over the trust-domain prefix (or two different BinStore instances behind a decorator). Every append succeeds, every 202 is returned, every commit is durable -- and every consumer 404s on the segment key the delta names, because those bytes live under the other prefix. No assertion, gate or metric distinguishes this from a healthy pod.

findings.summary: The ingester now holds a lease for its entire lifetime and nothing renews it. LocalSequencer never calls LeaseManager.renew(), DefaultIngest starts no renew tick beside its pusher/flusher threads, and no backlog row owns one (grep for renew finds M4.3b/d/g/h, all about LeaseManager's own mechanics). Before this change DefaultIngest held no lease at all, so this is a liveness obligation the diff acquires without discharging. Safety is untouched -- ADR-0002 makes the lease liveness only, and LocalSequencer.commit does not consult it -- so nothing fails today; it is stated here because this commit is what makes the ingester the holder, and because M4.6c's residue is easier to record now than to rediscover during the wiring commit.
findings.failure_scenario: The wiring commit ships two pods with a periodic election tick. Pod A sequences; its lease lapses one TTL after LocalSequencer.start because nothing renews it; pod B's tick acquires, seals A's chain and opens its own. A's next flush throws the fenced exception and fails every producer waiting on that batch -- a full failover on a perfectly healthy leader, repeating every TTL.

findings.summary: `flushSeq` is a plain instance field starting at 0, so a pod restart restarts the counter. Its javadoc calls it "Half the idempotency key, with podId (M4.10)" and CommitRequest's javadoc claims the pair "identifies this commit uniquely across the fleet", but podShortId is stable across restarts by construction (a StatefulSet pod's short id is exactly that), so (podId, 0), (podId, 1) ... are reissued after every restart. Nothing detects it today because Sequencer's contract states plainly that idempotency does not hold until M4.10 -- but the SHAPE M4.10 must dedupe on is chosen here, and the javadoc asserts a uniqueness the field does not have. The epoch, or a per-process nonce, is what would make the pair unique.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.10 implements replay suppression on (podId, flushSeq) exactly as CommitRequest specifies. The first N flushes after every pod restart carry keys the log has already applied and are suppressed as replays: producers are acked against offsets from the PREVIOUS process's deltas, or the commits are dropped outright. The bug surfaces inside M4.10's commit and reads as M4.10's defect, with nothing pointing back to the counter's lifetime being chosen here.

findings.summary: Two backlog edits ride along that are not M4.6d. (a) The new M4.6f row is inserted at line 267, between M4.14 and M4.15, while M4.6a-M4.6e sit together at lines 256-258 above M4.7 -- so the row that exists to delete a constructor "before the next wiring commit reaches it by accident" is ordered after M4.7's batching, M4.8's checkpoints and M4.9's bounded recovery, all of which will be built on top of that constructor. (b) M4.6c's status is changed from todo to "**done** (`3a5ed79`)" at line 256: a correct bookkeeping fix for an already-landed commit, but it is a second task's row edited under this task ID, which is the one-task-one-commit property AGENTS.md non-negotiable 1 asks for. Worth a line in the commit body rather than being left silent.
findings.failure_scenario: The next-task skill and a human both read the current-milestone table top-down. M4.6f, sitting 9 rows below where its family is, is either scheduled last -- after three tasks have been written against the 2-arg constructor it exists to remove -- or is missed entirely by someone scanning the M4.6 block for outstanding residue, which is exactly the reading the M4.6d row's own "the residue is M4.6f" sentence invites.

notes: Scope: the diff does route DefaultIngest through a Sequencer and deletes the 2-arg `new CommitLog` from production -- verified, `grep -rn 'new CommitLog('` leaves no main-source 2-arg site (ChainReplay and LocalSequencer all pass an explicit epoch), and the M4.6f row's counts check out exactly (18 two-arg sites in 5 files: CommitLogTest 13, EndToEndTest 2, SearchableIT 1, ShardFanOutIT 1, SubscriptionHubTest 1). All ten `new DefaultIngest` sites are tests, as the row claims. COST, judged rather than assumed: the added shutdown request is one putIfMatch inside LeaseManager.releaseLocked, reached once per DefaultIngest.close(), i.e. once per pod lifetime -- it scales with nodes, not with records, shards, partitions or indices, so cost.md R1-R11 are untouched and the 4->5 threshold move is genuinely justified rather than relaxed to make a test pass. It is also idempotent: release() returns before any I/O when belief == null, so a double close costs nothing. Per-flush cost is unchanged (sequencer.commit delegates to the same log.commit, one conditional PUT). The per-restart cost DID grow -- start now pays 2 lease requests, a SEAL PUT, a CONTINUE PUT and a transitive ancestor replay -- but that is M4.6e's, already recorded in its row and in LocalSequencer's javadoc, and it is per node per restart. The claim in DefaultIngest:150-153 that the startup-latency note "moved WITH the responsibility to LocalSequencer.start" is true: LocalSequencer:97-108 carries it verbatim. Module layering is sound: sequencer/src/testFixtures is the right home (FakeSequencer already lives there, and TestSequencers builds sequencer types), it adds no production dependency anywhere, and architecture.md rule 2 is not breached because plugin's clusterTest already carries :ingest and :binstore-backends while sequencer pulls only binstore-spi + format. Rule 4 (nothing depends on http) and rule 5 (no module below http references HTTP) are unaffected. Also checked and NOT flagged: the plugin ITs' move from epoch 0 to a leased epoch is invisible to the consumer, which never reads the commit log (no ctl/log or epoch reference anywhere in client/src/main); podShortId is still validated for '-' and '/' at construction by SegmentPublisher, so CommitRequest's stricter check is not a newly-deferred failure; and no commit can be issued after sequencer.close(), because the flusher only ever evaluates its loop condition while holding the lock that close() sets `closed` under.
